name: ucp-audit
tagline: Is your shop reachable by AI shopping agents?
search: Universal Commerce Protocol readiness, /.well-known/ucp check, agentic commerce merchant audit, why AI agents do not show my products
summary: Google and Shopify's Universal Commerce Protocol lets AI agents shop: every business publishes a machine-readable profile at /.well-known/ucp and agents read it to decide what they can do with that shop. The failure mode is silence - offer checkout without declaring a searchable catalogue and no agent will ever surface your products, with no error page and no warning anywhere.
how: Reads the profile the way an agent does and reports what an agent would conclude.
Catches the case that matters most: checkout offered while catalog.search and catalog.lookup are missing, so an agent can pay for what it already knows about and discover nothing.

Finds the contradictions a profile carries silently - a capability requiring a newer protocol than the profile declares, an extends pointing at a capability that is not offered, a plaintext endpoint, a transport with nowhere to send a request.
Compares your protocol version against the published spec, because each release has added shopping capabilities.
proof: Run against chewy.com on the day it was written: checkout, fulfilment and order declared, neither catalogue capability, protocol seven months behind. allbirds.com the same day: eight capabilities on the current version. Both profiles are recorded in the repository as test fixtures.

name: cra-report
tagline: EU Cyber Resilience Act Article 14 reporting tool
search: CRA Article 14 reporting tool, actively exploited vulnerability 24 hours, ENISA notification, SBOM KEV cross-reference
summary: Since 11 September 2026 a manufacturer placing a product with digital elements on the EU market has 24 hours to notify ENISA of an actively exploited vulnerability in it. Finding vulnerabilities is not the hard part - any scanner hands you a hundred. cra-report says which of them starts the statutory clock, and drafts the Article 14 notification for the ones that do.
how: Reads a CycloneDX or SPDX SBOM, package-lock.json, Cargo.lock or a pinned requirements.txt.
Asks OSV what is known about those exact versions, across npm, PyPI, crates.io, Go, Maven, NuGet, RubyGems and Packagist.
Cross-references every CVE against the CISA KEV catalogue - the list of vulnerabilities observed being exploited in the wild.
Writes the Article 14(1) early warning with both deadlines counted from now, and marks what only a person can answer.
proof: On a dependency tree containing log4j-core 2.14.1 it reports 2 findings with a deadline out of 19 advisories, both flagged as used in ransomware campaigns. On lodash 4.17.15 it reports 0 out of 6 - equally worth being able to say.

name: well-known-audit
tagline: Every file your site publishes at its root, checked at once
search: security.txt expired check, RFC 9116 Expires validator, well-known files audit, llms.txt robots.txt assetlinks checker
summary: A site publishes a dozen small files at its root and under /.well-known/ that nobody owns: security.txt, robots.txt, llms.txt, assetlinks.json, apple-app-site-association, mta-sts.txt and the rest. Each one is checked by a different tool, or by nobody. This reads all of them in one run and says which are missing, which are malformed, and which have quietly expired - starting with security.txt, whose Expires field makes the file formally invalid once the date passes.
how: Reads twelve well-known and root files in one pass, four requests at a time, and reports them together.
Validates security.txt against RFC 9116: a Contact line is required, an Expires line is required, and a date in the past means the file is no longer valid - it counts the days either way.
Catches the common silent failure: apple-app-site-association or assetlinks.json served as HTML, which iOS and Android quietly ignore.
Refuses private and loopback addresses, checks every redirect hop rather than the first URL, and stops reading a body at 5 MB.
Audits a list of domains in one run and writes the totals as CSV, one polite domain at a time.
proof: Run against the Tranco top 500 on 2026-09-18: of the 158 sites that publish a security.txt, 92 have no Expires field at all and 6 have expired - nearly two thirds are invalid under RFC 9116. Four of the flagged sites were checked by hand with curl before the number was published. 106 tests, none of which touch a network.

name: webhook-rewind
tagline: Record webhooks once, replay them re-signed
search: replay webhook locally, re-sign webhook signature, test Stripe Shopify WhatsApp webhook without provider
summary: A webhook handler breaks in production and you need the payload that broke it. The provider will send you the next event, not that one. A payload copied out of a log fails signature verification, because every provider signs the raw bytes. webhook-rewind keeps the body as bytes from capture to replay and re-signs it with your own secret.
how: Captures every inbound request to a JSON Lines file, answering 200 immediately so the provider does not back off.
Re-signs on replay for Meta (WhatsApp, Instagram, Messenger), GitHub, Shopify and Stripe.
Gives Stripe a fresh timestamp, because its tolerance window rejects the recorded one.
Redacts Authorization, Cookie and API-key headers before anything reaches disk.
proof: Every signing scheme is checked against an independent implementation of the verifying side, not against a frozen digest. 35 tests, none of which touch a network.

name: api-drift
tagline: Catch a partner API changing shape before it breaks you
search: detect API response schema change, API contract monitoring, breaking change detection JSON
summary: Integrations rarely break loudly. A partner renames order_id to orderId, or starts sending total as a number, and nothing throws - the field reads as undefined and a fortnight of rows go out empty before anyone notices. api-drift records the shape of a response and tells you when it changes.
how: Infers a schema from one or several sample responses, so a sometimes-absent field is recorded as optional rather than becoming tomorrow's false alarm.
Classifies each change from the point of view of code that already consumes the old shape: removed field, changed type, became nullable and became optional are breaking; a new field is not.
Stores the baseline as one JSON file with sorted keys, meant to be committed - so the change shows up in code review.
Treats a non-2xx answer or a non-JSON body as an outage, not as drift.
proof: Reproducible from two fixtures in the repository: it reports a rename as its two halves, a string that became a number, and a value that can now be null.

name: csvdiff
tagline: Diff two CSV exports by key and see what actually changed
search: compare two CSV files by key, data migration verification, CSV diff tool large files
summary: "The data does not match after the migration" is a week of work, and it always starts with two exports and a spreadsheet. csvdiff compares them by key and reports what moved, per column, with the transitions counted.
how: Two million rows, 131 MB, in 2.8 seconds, holding about 60 bytes per row of the old file.
Treats 1000, 1000.00 and 1.000,00 as one value, and empty, NULL, NaN and \N as one nothing - while keeping the cents in money.
Calls out broken rows and duplicate keys instead of quietly diffing them.
Exit code 1 when anything differs, so it works as a gate.
proof: The benchmark is a script in the repository: it builds both exports from a fixed seed, so the timing repeats on any machine.
stack: prebuilt binaries for Linux, macOS and Windows

name: leakscan
tagline: See what leaves with a file before you send it
search: check document for hidden data before sending, tracked changes deleted text, EXIF GPS in photos, hidden worksheet
summary: An offline check of everything a file carries that you did not mean to send: tracked changes with the deleted text still readable, review comments, worksheets hidden at the veryHidden level, attachments inside a PDF, GPS coordinates in photos, and validated card and IBAN numbers.
how: Reads the file formats directly - no network access at any point, so it is safe on material that must not leave the machine.
Validates card and IBAN numbers rather than matching digit patterns, which is the difference between a finding and noise.
Reports what it found and where, and changes nothing.
proof: 41 tests across office documents, PDFs and images.

name: invoice-reconciler
tagline: Match a bank statement against open invoices
search: reconcile bank statement with invoices automatically, payment matching script, part payment batch transfer
summary: Matches payments to invoices in five passes - references, part payments, batch transfers, instalments - and reports only what does not add up. The cases that make manual reconciliation slow are the ones it is built around.
how: Detects the date convention of each file rather than assuming one.
Drops a shortfall that a later payment covered, instead of reporting it twice.
Writes the exception list as CSV or JSON for whoever has to chase it.
proof: Standard library only: it runs on any Python 3.10+ with nothing installed.

name: whatsapp-crm-connector
tagline: WhatsApp Business Cloud webhooks into a CRM
search: WhatsApp Cloud API webhook to CRM, verify X-Hub-Signature-256, 24 hour window token refresh
summary: The parts of a WhatsApp integration that are not the happy path: signature verification, an instant acknowledgement with the work moved to a queue, de-duplication of repeated deliveries, conversations logged against both the contact and the company, the 24-hour window, and token refresh.
how: Verifies the Meta signature over the raw body, and rejects a forged one.
Answers within milliseconds and processes afterwards, because Meta retries anything slow.
Runs offline with one command, against recorded payloads.
proof: 42 tests, including a forged signature that must be refused.

name: email-deliverability-check
tagline: Find out why a domain's mail lands in spam
search: why emails go to spam, SPF too many lookups, DMARC p=none, DKIM revoked, MTA-STS missing
summary: Checks the things that actually put mail in the spam folder: the SPF ten-lookup limit, duplicated records, DKIM keys that have been revoked, DMARC stuck at p=none, and a missing MTA-STS policy. DNS only - no access to the mailbox is needed, which makes it usable on a prospect's domain.
how: Resolves and counts SPF lookups the way a receiving server does.
Batch mode for a list of client domains, with CSV output.
proof: 17 offline checks over recorded DNS answers.
